## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 3: matching **discards** people and targets the **ATT**
- Today: **weighting** keeps **everybody** and can target the **ATE**
- By the end you can:
  - build **inverse probability weights** and check them
  - estimate the **ATE** and the **ATT** with a **robust SE**
  - combine weights with an outcome model (**doubly robust**)
:::

# Topic 1 — The weights {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Inverse probability of the option received

::: {.eq}
enrolled: w = 1 / PS      not enrolled: w = 1 / (1 − PS)
:::

```{r}
htn$w <- ifelse(htn$programme == 1, 1 / htn$ps, 1 / (1 - htn$ps))
pt <- mean(htn$programme)
htn$sw <- ifelse(htn$programme == 1, pt / htn$ps, (1 - pt) / (1 - htn$ps))
rbind(unstabilised = summary(htn$w), stabilised = summary(htn$sw)) |> round(2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- An adult who enrolled **against the odds** (PS 0.1) stands for **10** similar adults: weight 10
- The weighted sample is a **pseudo-population** in which enrolment is **unrelated to the confounders**: like a trial
- **Stabilised** weights (multiplied by the overall probability) have **mean 1** and a smaller range (**0.42 to 6.2** instead of up to 15)
:::

## Balance after weighting

```{r}
bal.tab(f_ps, data = htn, weights = "sw", un = TRUE, s.d.denom = "pooled")$Balance[, c("Diff.Un", "Diff.Adj")] |> round(2)
```

All SMDs are **0.03 or less**: the same check as for matching. If not, **improve the propensity model**.

# Topic 2 — The effect {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## ATE with a robust SE

```{r}
fit_w <- lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn, weights = sw)
round(coeftest(fit_w, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_w, type = "HC3"))["programme", 1:2], 2)
```

::: {.key}
**ATE −5.7 mmHg** (robust SE 0.55); the truth is **−5.8**. A **robust (sandwich) SE** is needed: weighted observations do not count equally and the weights are **estimated**. The bootstrap is the alternative.
:::

## ATT weights

```{r}
htn$w_att <- ifelse(htn$programme == 1, 1, htn$ps / (1 - htn$ps))
fit_att <- lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn, weights = w_att)
round(coeftest(fit_att, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_att, type = "HC3"))["programme", 1:2], 2)
```

Enrolled adults keep weight **1**; the others are re-weighted to **look like the enrolled** (PS / (1 − PS)). **ATT −6.6 mmHg**: larger than the ATE, as in Session 2.

## Extreme weights

```{r}
q <- quantile(htn$sw, c(0.01, 0.99)); htn$sw_t <- pmin(pmax(htn$sw, q[1]), q[2])
round(c(ipw = coef(fit_w)[["programme"]], truncated = coef(lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn, weights = sw_t))[["programme"]]), 2)
```

::: {.warn}
A few **very large weights** make the estimate **unstable** and signal **poor overlap**. **Look at them** (who are these people?). **Truncating** at the 1st and 99th percentile trades a little bias for stability: here **−5.7 → −5.6**, so the result does not rest on a few adults.
:::

# Topic 3 — Doubly robust {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Weights plus an outcome model

```{r}
fit_dr <- lm(f_out, data = htn, weights = sw)
round(coeftest(fit_dr, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_dr, type = "HC3"))["programme", 1:2], 2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **−6.0 mmHg** (SE 0.46): **more precise**
- **Doubly robust**: consistent if **either** the propensity model **or** the outcome model is right
- It does **not** protect against **unmeasured** confounding
:::

## All the estimates

```{r}
round(c(naive = coef(lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn))[["programme"]], regression = coef(lm(f_out, data = htn))[["programme"]], ipw = coef(fit_w)[["programme"]], doubly_robust = coef(fit_dr)[["programme"]]), 2)
```

::: {.key}
Regression **−6.3**, matching **−5.9**, IPW **−5.7**, doubly robust **−6.0**; truth **−5.8**. Methods that use the **same confounders** agree. **Agreement is reassuring, but it is not proof**: they all share the assumption of **no unmeasured confounding**.
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("z4q1", "An adult with a propensity score of 0.1 enrolled in the programme. What is the unstabilised weight, and why?",
         c("10, since this adult stands for ten similar adults in the population",
           "0.1, since adults who are unlikely to enrol should count for less in the analysis",
           "1.1, since the weight is one plus the propensity score of the adult",
           "0.9, since the weight is the chance of not being enrolled in the programme"), answer = 1,
         explain = "The weight is one divided by the probability of the option actually received. Unlikely choices are rare in the data and so are weighted up.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("z4q2", "What does weighting create?",
         c("A smaller sample that contains matched pairs of similar adults from both groups",
           "A pseudo-population where exposure is unrelated to measured confounders",
           "A dataset in which every adult has the same predicted outcome at twelve months",
           "A population in which the unmeasured confounders are balanced as well"), answer = 2,
         explain = "After weighting, confounders have the same distribution in both groups, as they would after randomisation. Unmeasured confounders are not addressed.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("z4q3", "Why use a robust (sandwich) standard error with inverse probability weights?",
         c("The robust standard error is smaller than the model-based standard error",
           "The outcome is not normally distributed in the weighted sample of adults",
           "Robust standard errors remove the bias from unmeasured confounding",
           "Weighted observations count unequally, and the weights are estimated"), answer = 4,
         explain = "The usual model-based SE treats weights as known frequencies, which is wrong. The sandwich estimator, or a bootstrap, gives valid inference.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("z4q4", "A few adults have very large weights. What is the right response?",
         c("Examine them, check overlap, and consider truncating the weights",
           "Delete those adults and report the analysis of the remaining ones",
           "Ignore it, because large weights make the estimate more precise",
           "Multiply all the weights by a constant to make them smaller"), answer = 1,
         explain = "Large weights indicate adults with few comparable counterparts. They make estimates unstable; truncation trades a little bias for stability, and should be reported.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("z4q5", "What does 'doubly robust' mean?",
         c("It is protected against both measured and unmeasured confounding alike",
           "The analysis was repeated twice with two different random seeds",
           "It is consistent if the propensity or outcome model is right",
           "The standard error is computed by two different robust methods"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Combining weights with an outcome model gives two chances to model the confounding correctly. Neither helps if a confounder was not measured.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **IPW**: weight = 1 / P(option received); **stabilise**
- Check **balance** and the **weight distribution**
- **Robust SE** (or bootstrap)
- ATE and **ATT** need different weights
- **Doubly robust** = weights + outcome model; still no cure for unmeasured confounding
:::
